builder_plan.scenario: An assistant chooses the wrong API or sends arguments your product cannot use.
builder_plan.change: Apply the proposed tool-selection or argument-generation change in a sandbox.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current agent with the same tool schemas and task budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct completed actions, invalid calls, retries, latency, and cost per completed task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: One Task, Many Interfaces: Simple Cross-Interface Consistency Training Improves LLM Agent Robustness
summary: CIPR augments standard SFT or RL post-training, where each sample is scored independently under one interface, with a self-supervised KL penalty between action distributions produced under two interface views of the same sample in which action names are replaced by uninformative identifiers. It costs the construction of paired interface views and an additional forward pass per training sample to compute the cross-interface KL, but adds no inference-time latency or memory overhead. It can fail when held-out perturbations fall outside the consistency structure learned during training, it recovers only part of the robustness gap (10.5 of roughly 25 points), and it is inapplicable to teams that consume models exclusively through inference APIs without fine-tuning access.
rationale: The method is a lightweight training-time regularizer implementable on a single GPU for teams that fine-tune their own function-calling agents, but its partial recovery of the robustness gap and dependence on the training interface distribution require validation on the reader's specific tool schemas before production adoption.
technique: Cross-Interface Policy Regularization (CIPR) for tool-use agents

claims.statement: CIPR augments standard SFT or RL post-training, where each sample is scored independently under one interface, with a self-supervised KL penalty between action distributions produced under two interface views of the same sample in which action names are replaced by uninformative identifiers. It costs the construction of paired interface views and an additional forward pass per training sample to compute the cross-interface KL, but adds no inference-time latency or memory overhead. It can fail when held-out perturbations fall outside the consistency structure learned during training, it recovers only part of the robustness gap (10.5 of roughly 25 points), and it is inapplicable to teams that consume models exclusively through inference APIs without fine-tuning access.

On agentic function calling, held-out interface perturbations reduce post-trained agent accuracy by nearly 25%, and CIPR recovers 10.5 percentage points of that drop while leaving accuracy on the unchanged interface intact.
